i18n.en: And it came to pass after these things, that the Elohim tested Avraham, and said to him, Avraham. And he said, Here am I.

notes.official:
*Nisah* — the piel of *n-s-h*, *to test, try, put to the test* — is the chapter's defining narrator-comment and one of the most theologically-discussed verses in the entire Hebrew Bible. The narrator preempts the reader's misreading of v 2 by naming the entire pericope a *test* before it begins; the dramatic-irony of the chapter is structurally generated by this opening (see [nisah-divine-testing](#nisah-divine-testing) for the full lexeme-and-distribution survey).

Gen 22:1 is the **first occurrence of the divine-testing piel in the Hebrew Bible** and the only patriarchal-narrative instance; the motif is otherwise concentrated in the Mosaic and post-Mosaic corpus (Exod 15:25 the bitter-waters at Marah; Exod 16:4 the manna; Exod 20:20 Sinai post-theophany; Deut 8:2, 8:16, 13:4, 33:8; Judg 2:22, 3:1, 3:4; Ps 26:2; 2 Chr 32:31).

The theological-problem the verse generates — *if the deity is omniscient, what does the test produce?* — is one of the most-discussed cruxes of the Hebrew Bible reception-history. Four scholarly positions parallel: **Maimonides** (*Guide* III.24) reads the test as pedagogical-demonstration *l-hodi'a* (to make known) to humanity; **Augustine** and the patristic tradition read the test as disclosing the latent disposition in publicly-visible form; the modern philosophical-theology *open theism* position (Pinnock, Sanders, Boyd) reads the test as genuinely producing new divine knowledge; the modern critical default (Sarna, Westermann, Wenham, Hamilton, Brueggemann) reads the *atah yadati* of v 12 and the *nisah* of v 1 as narrative-anthropomorphism — the chapter is a story in the strict literary sense, and the story requires the test-and-discover narrative-grammar. The four positions are documented; none is preempted at the translation level. See [nisah-divine-testing](#nisah-divine-testing) and [ata-yadati-divine-learning-question](#ata-yadati-divine-learning-question) for the full apparatus.

The article-bearing *ha-Elohim* (rather than bare *Elohim* or *YHWH*) is editorially significant: across the chapter the divine-name distribution is load-bearing — *ha-Elohim* at vv 1, 3, 9 for the test-commanding figure; bare *Elohim* at v 8 (Avraham's reply) and v 12 (*yere Elohim* certification); *YHWH* at vv 11, 14, 15, 16 for the staying-of-the-hand, the place-name, and the oath. The classical source-critical reading (Gunkel, von Rad, Westermann) treats this as an E-J redactional fingerprint with the J supplement at vv 11b-18 carrying the YHWH name. The WoH article-convention renders the form *the Elohim* per [elohim-as-translation](#elohim-as-translation).

The first of the chapter's threefold *hineni* (vv 1, 7, 11) opens here — the prophetic-response formula in the call-narrative type-scene (Habel ZAW 1965; Brueggemann 1982). See [hineni-prophetic-response-formula](#hineni-prophetic-response-formula).

The wider philosophical reception (Kierkegaard *Fear and Trembling* 1843; Auerbach *Mimesis* 1946 ch. 1; Derrida *The Gift of Death* 1995) and the rabbinic-liturgical reception (Spiegel *The Last Trial* 1967; Levenson *The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son* 1993) are flagged as downstream-not-preempted.

i18n.en: And he said, Take now your son, your only son, whom you love, even Yitzchaq, and go forth to the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt-offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell you of.

notes.official:
The chapter's pivot-command. Four lexical-and-philological cruxes converge in a single verse, each of which carries reception-history beyond what the translation can preempt.

***Qach-na et-binkha et-yechidkha asher ahavta et-Yitzchaq***. The command's slow accumulation — *take now your son, your only one, whom you love, [namely] Yitzchaq* — is editorially deliberate. **Rashi** (citing Genesis Rabbah 39:9 and 55:7) reads the four-fold designation as a dramatic-prolongation: Avraham asks at each stage *which son?* — *your son* (*I have two*), *your only one* (*each is the only one of his mother*), *whom you love* (*I love them both*), until the final naming *Yitzchaq* leaves no escape. The midrashic reading captures the verse's deliberate-prolongation effect, which the modern critical literature (Sarna, Alter) reaches on literary-narrative grounds without the midrashic dramatization.

*Yechidkha* — *your only one* — generates a narrative-internal tension: Yitzchaq is not Avraham's only son. Yishma'el was born at Gen 16, expelled at Gen 21:8-21 but not dead. The modern critical readings — Yitzchaq as the *only-one-of-the-promise-line* per Gen 21:12 (Sarna 1989 p. 151; Wenham 1994 p. 105; Hamilton 1995 p. 105); *yechid* in the affective-emotional sense *beloved-because-unique* (Levenson 1993 pp. 28-34); the combined reading — are parallel; the verse does not require disambiguation. The downstream Christian (Vulgate *unigenitum*, the Johannine *monogenes* echo at John 3:16, Hebrews 11:17-19) and Islamic (Quran 37:101-113, with the early tafsir tradition divided on Yitzchaq vs. Yishma'el and the dominant Sunni Yishma'el-identification documented in Firestone 1990) receptions are flagged-not-preempted. See [yechid-only-one-formula](#yechid-only-one-formula). The cross-corpus distribution (Judg 11:34 Jephthah's daughter; Ps 22:21, 35:17; Zech 12:10 the pierced-one with NT-reception at John 19:37) is also in the entry.

***Lekh-lekha el eretz ha-Moriah***. The doubled-imperative *lekh-lekha* (*go forth*) recurs here as the second and final use in the Hebrew Bible — the first being Gen 12:1, the call-of-Avram. The two uses form a deliberate inclusio across the Abraham-cycle (Sarna, Alter); see [lekh-lekha](#lekh-lekha) for the full ethical-dative discussion.

*Eretz ha-Moriah* — *the land of Moriah* — is a Pentateuchal hapax (the noun recurs only once more in the entire Hebrew Bible, at 2 Chr 3:1, where the Chronicler explicitly identifies *har ha-Moriah* with the Jerusalem Temple Mount). The Chronicler's identification is the foundation of the Jewish tradition (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan; Rashi; Maimonides). Modern critical scholarship is divided: **Sarna** 1989 p. 151 accepts the 2 Chr 3:1 identification as preserving ancient tradition; **Westermann** 1985 p. 357 and **Speiser** 1964 p. 163 read the Chronicler as retrojecting. The textual variants are significant — **LXX** *eis tēn gēn tēn hypsēlēn* (*into the high land*) suggests a different Vorlage or interpretive gloss; **Samaritan Pentateuch** *eretz ha-Moreh* connects the site to the *elon Moreh* of Shechem and supports the Samaritan Mount-Gerizim identification. The MT *ha-Moriah* is preserved per WoH MT-fidelity policy; see [eretz-ha-moriah-temple-mount-identification](#eretz-ha-moriah-temple-mount-identification) for the full text-critical and reception-historical apparatus.

***V-ha'alehu sham l-olah***. *Olah* — *that-which-goes-up* / *whole-burnt-offering* — is the cultic-technical term for the principal sacrifice-class of Lev 1, the sacrifice entirely consumed by fire on the altar with the smoke ascending to the deity. The chapter is the first sustained narrative use of *olah* in the Hebrew Bible (six occurrences across the chapter at vv 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 13) and the first narrative use of *olah* with a human victim. The pre-Sinai pre-cultic-legislative status is editorially significant: the reader encounters *olah* here before the Sinai legislation that will codify the sacrificial system and explicitly prohibit human-sacrifice (Lev 18:21, 20:2-5; Deut 12:31, 18:10). On one mainstream reading (Levenson 1993; Sarna), the *aqedah*'s pre-Sinai non-completion of the human-*olah* is the foundational textual repudiation of child-sacrifice. See [olah-burnt-offering](#olah-burnt-offering) for the full cultic-technical-and-comparative apparatus including the ANE *molk* / *mlk* material (Day 1989; Heider 1985; Stager and Wolff 1984).

paragraphs.text: וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם אַבְרָהָ֜ם בַּבֹּ֗קֶר וַֽיַּחֲבֹשׁ֙ אֶת־חֲמֹר֔וֹ וַיִּקַּ֞ח אֶת־שְׁנֵ֤י נְעָרָיו֙ אִתּ֔וֹ וְאֵ֖ת יִצְחָ֣ק בְּנ֑וֹ וַיְבַקַּע֙ עֲצֵ֣י עֹלָ֔ה וַיָּ֣קָם וַיֵּ֔לֶךְ אֶל־הַמָּק֖וֹם אֲשֶׁר־אָֽמַר־ל֥וֹ הָאֱלֹהִֽים׃

i18n.en: And Avraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Yitzchaq his son; and he split the wood for the burnt-offering, and rose up, and went to the place of which the Elohim had told him.

paragraphs.text: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֗י וַיִּשָּׂ֨א אַבְרָהָ֧ם אֶת־עֵינָ֛יו וַיַּ֥רְא אֶת־הַמָּק֖וֹם מֵרָחֹֽק׃

i18n.en: On the third day Avraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place afar off.

notes.official:
*Ba-yom ha-shlishi* — *on the third day* — is a Hebrew Bible stylized-formulaic marker for theophany, decisive-event, or transition. The modern critical literature (Sarna 1989 p. 152; Westermann 1985 p. 358; Wenham 1994 p. 107; Alter 2004 p. 110) reads it as a literary-narrative convention rather than as a literal chronometric datum.

The cross-corpus distribution makes the *third-day* a stylized topos: Exod 19:11, 15-16 (the Sinai theophany — the parallel-most-cited cross-reference for Gen 22); **Hos 6:2** (*on the third day he will raise us up* — the keystone cross-corpus verse for the *third-day-resurrection* motif); Esth 5:1 (Esther's decisive intervention); Jonah 1:17 / MT 2:1 (the three-days-and-three-nights in the fish, cited at Matt 12:40); and Gen 31:22, 34:25, 40:20, 42:18 within the Genesis corpus itself.

The **NT-resurrection-typology** (1 Cor 15:4; Luke 24:7, 21, 46; Matt 12:40; Acts 10:40) reads the Gen 22 third-day prefiguratively; the patristic-typology (Origen, Augustine, Tertullian) treats Yitzchaq's *bound-but-not-slain* on the third day as the typological prefiguration of the *crucified-but-raised* on the third day (Daly 1978; Lerch 1950). The **Jewish-liturgical reception** is equally rich — the *Akedah* is read on Rosh Hashanah; the *zechut avot* (merit of the fathers) tradition treats the third-day-arrival as the foundational moment of merit-imputation (Spiegel 1967; Levenson 1993 chs 8-10). Both reception-traditions are flagged-not-preempted by [ba-yom-ha-shlishi-third-day-formula](#ba-yom-ha-shlishi-third-day-formula).

The *sa eynav va-yar* (*lifted up his eyes and saw*) formula is the patriarchal seeing-and-perception formula (see [sa-eynekha-lift-your-eyes](#sa-eynekha-lift-your-eyes)). The chapter's first use of the formula; the second at v 13 (Avraham seeing the substitute ram) frames the chapter's structural seeing-arc.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אַבְרָהָ֜ם אֶל־נְעָרָ֗יו שְׁבוּ־לָכֶ֥ם פֹּה֙ עִֽם־הַחֲמ֔וֹר וַאֲנִ֣י וְהַנַּ֔עַר נֵלְכָ֖ה עַד־כֹּ֑ה וְנִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֖ה וְנָשׁ֥וּבָה אֲלֵיכֶֽם׃

i18n.en: And Avraham said to his young men, Stay here with the donkey, and I and the lad will go yonder; and we will worship, and come again to you.

notes.official:
*V-nashuvah aleykhem* — *and we will come again to you* — uses the plural verb (Avraham and Yitzchaq both subjects). The plural is grammatically explicit and editorially significant. **Rashi** (Bereshit Rabbah 56:2) reads it as Avraham's prophetic confidence that Yitzchaq will return — i.e., implicit faith in resurrection or substitution. **Hebrews 11:19** makes the resurrection-typology explicit: *logisamenos hoti kai ek nekrōn egeirein dynatos ho theos, hothen auton kai en parabolē ekomisato* — *reasoning that God was able to raise [him] even from the dead, from which he did receive him back as a parable*.

Modern critical scholarship (Sarna 1989 p. 152; Wenham 1994 p. 108; Hamilton 1995 p. 110) parallel three readings: (a) deliberate dramatic-irony of the narrator; (b) Avraham's protective speech to the young men, concealing the test from them; (c) latent faith in a non-final outcome. The translation does not need to disambiguate — the plural is grammatically explicit. The Hebrews-typology is downstream-reception, flagged-not-preempted.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֨ח אַבְרָהָ֜ם אֶת־עֲצֵ֣י הָעֹלָ֗ה וַיָּ֙שֶׂם֙ עַל־יִצְחָ֣ק בְּנ֔וֹ וַיִּקַּ֣ח בְּיָד֔וֹ אֶת־הָאֵ֖שׁ וְאֶת־הַֽמַּאֲכֶ֑לֶת וַיֵּלְכ֥וּ שְׁנֵיהֶ֖ם יַחְדָּֽו׃

i18n.en: And Avraham took the wood of the burnt-offering, and laid it on Yitzchaq his son; and he took in his hand the fire and the knife; and they went both of them together.

notes.official:
*Ma'akhelet* — *the slaughter-knife / large-eating-knife* — is one of the chapter's most marked-rare lexemes. The noun recurs only three times in the entire Hebrew Bible (here at Gen 22:6 + v 10; Judg 19:29 the Levite's dismembering-knife for the concubine; Prov 30:14 the metaphorical *jaw-teeth as knives*). The chapter's two occurrences (v 6 loading-of-implements; v 10 the narrative-climax) mark the chapter's vocabulary for the act of slaughter as specialized. **Sarna** 1989 p. 152: *the rare term ma'akhelet, the slaughtering-knife, intensifies the dramatic horror*. **Alter** 2004 p. 110: *the rare slaughter-knife*. **Hamilton** 1995 p. 110: *the term often refers to a larger knife or even a sword*. See [ma-akhelet-sacrificial-knife](#ma-akhelet-sacrificial-knife).

The verse-closing *va-yelkhu shneihem yachdav* — *and they went, the two of them, together* — recurs at v 8b, framing the father-and-son walking-together as the chapter's most affectively-weighted refrain (Sarna 1989; Alter 2004 p. 110).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יִצְחָ֜ק אֶל־אַבְרָהָ֤ם אָבִיו֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אָבִ֔י וַיֹּ֖אמֶר הִנֶּ֣נִּֽי בְנִ֑י וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הִנֵּ֤ה הָאֵשׁ֙ וְהָ֣עֵצִ֔ים וְאַיֵּ֥ה הַשֶּׂ֖ה לְעֹלָֽה׃

i18n.en: And Yitzchaq spoke to Avraham his father, and said, My father. And he said, Here am I, my son. And he said, Behold, the fire and the wood; but where is the lamb for a burnt-offering?

notes.official:
The chapter's middle *hineni*. Yitzchaq calls — *Avi* (*my father*) — and Avraham responds *hineni v'ni* (*here am I, my son*). The doubled-affective vocative (father–son; son–father) is the chapter's most affectively-weighted moment: Yitzchaq does not yet know what is happening, and Avraham's *hineni* to the son is grammatically the same response-formula he gave to the deity at v 1 and will give to the messenger at v 11.

The threefold-*hineni* structure (vv 1, 7, 11) is one of the chapter's most-cited compositional features. **Sarna** 1989 p. 150: *the threefold hineni gives the chapter its structural-rhythmic backbone*. **Alter** 2004 p. 109: *the three hineni-responses, each in a different vocative direction, anchor the chapter's three-fold structure*. See [hineni-prophetic-response-formula](#hineni-prophetic-response-formula) for the cross-corpus prophetic-vocational distribution (Gen 31:11; 37:13; 46:2 — the *Ya'aqov Ya'aqov* doublet; Exod 3:4 — Moshe at the burning bush; 1 Sam 3 — Sh'mu'el's fourfold call; Isa 6:8 — Isaiah's *here am I, send me*).

Yitzchaq's question — *v-ayeh ha-seh l-olah* (*but where is the lamb for a burnt-offering*) — is the chapter's most-quoted line. The question is grammatically straightforward but narratively-devastating: the son names the missing element (the *seh* — the lamb / kid) that he himself, by the narrative's logic, is to become.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ אַבְרָהָ֔ם אֱלֹהִ֞ים יִרְאֶה־לּ֥וֹ הַשֶּׂ֛ה לְעֹלָ֖ה בְּנִ֑י וַיֵּלְכ֥וּ שְׁנֵיהֶ֖ם יַחְדָּֽו׃

i18n.en: And Avraham said, Elohim will provide himself the lamb for a burnt-offering, my son: so they went both of them together.

notes.official:
*Elohim yir'eh-lo ha-seh* — *Elohim will see for himself / provide for himself the lamb*. The verb is the qal active 3ms imperfect of *r-'-h* (to see) with the reflexive *lamed* + 3ms suffix — *will see for himself*. The Hebrew preserves the seeing-equals-providing identity unambiguously; modern English does not (the etymological connection between *provide* and Latin *pro-videre*, *to see in advance*, is accidental — modern English readers do not hear *see* in *provide*).

The verse opens the chapter's wordplay-engine — the **r-'-h root play** that structures the chapter at vv 4, 8, 13, 14 (active *yir'eh*) and 14b (niphal passive *yera'eh*). The five-fold *r-'-h* axis is the chapter's deliberate compositional device (Sarna, Alter, Wenham, Hamilton — see [yireh-yerah-hreh-wordplay](#yireh-yerah-hreh-wordplay)).

Avraham's answer is grammatically ambiguous: it can be read as a faith-statement (*Elohim will provide* — Avraham trusts the deity to supply the substitute), as protective-deception of Yitzchaq (a cover for the test that Avraham has been forbidden to disclose), or as dramatic-irony (the narrator setting up the substitution-pivot at v 13 by foreshadowing the substitute-lamb in Avraham's own words). **Sarna** 1989 p. 152, **Alter** 2004 p. 110, and **Wenham** 1994 p. 108 parallel the three readings; the verse declines to disambiguate. The repeated refrain *va-yelkhu shneihem yachdav* (*and they went, the two of them, together*) closes the verse for the second time, framing the father-and-son's continued together-walking as the chapter's most affectively-weighted constant.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּבֹ֗אוּ אֶֽל־הַמָּקוֹם֮ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אָֽמַר־ל֣וֹ הָאֱלֹהִים֒ וַיִּ֨בֶן שָׁ֤ם אַבְרָהָם֙ אֶת־הַמִּזְבֵּ֔חַ וַֽיַּעֲרֹ֖ךְ אֶת־הָעֵצִ֑ים וַֽיַּעֲקֹד֙ אֶת־יִצְחָ֣ק בְּנ֔וֹ וַיָּ֤שֶׂם אֹתוֹ֙ עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּ֔חַ מִמַּ֖עַל לָעֵצִֽים׃

i18n.en: And they came to the place which the Elohim had told him of; and Avraham built the altar there, and laid the wood in order, and bound Yitzchaq his son, and laid him on the altar, upon the wood.

notes.official:
*Va-ya'aqod et-Yitzchaq* — *and he bound Yitzchaq*. The verb is the qal of *aqad* (to bind, truss) — a **Pentateuchal hapax** in the verbal form. The morphologically-related noun *aqudim* (*striped, ringed, banded*) recurs in the Jacob-flock-breeding narrative of Gen 30-31, but the qal verbal sense *to bind* is unique to this verse in the entire Pentateuch (the wider verbal root is attested in post-biblical and Mishnaic Hebrew, where the verbal sense is standard).

The verb's uniqueness is editorially load-bearing: the entire pericope is named *Aqedat Yitzchaq* (*the Binding of Yitzchaq*) in the post-biblical Jewish tradition from this verb. **Genesis Rabbah 56**; **b. Rosh Hashanah 16a, 26a**; **Mishnah Tamid 4:1** explicitly compares the daily *tamid*-offering's binding-procedure to Gen 22:9 — the front-right and rear-left legs bound together (forming the *aqedah*), the head-and-throat exposed for the *shechita*. The Mishnah cites Gen 22:9 as the precedent. Modern commentators (Sarna 1989 p. 153; Wenham 1994 p. 109; Hamilton 1995 p. 110) read the *aqad* verb as a technical-specialized sacrificial-binding term. See [aqad-bind-aqedah-hapax](#aqad-bind-aqedah-hapax) for the full lexeme-and-reception apparatus including the wider Semitic-cognate distribution (Akkadian *eqēdu*, Arabic *ʿaqada*).

The chapter's narrative-vocabulary is densely cultic-technical at this verse: *va-yiven sham Avraham et-ha-mizbeach* (*built the altar*) — the first patriarchal-altar-construction at this site; *va-ya'arokh et-ha-etzim* (*laid the wood in order*) — the verb *arakh* is itself the cultic-technical wood-arranging term of Lev 1:7, 8, 12; 6:5 (English 6:12). The narrator's vocabulary at v 9 saturates the verse with sacrificial-cultic technical terms, intensifying the (averted) horror through specialized-cultic language.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח אַבְרָהָם֙ אֶת־יָד֔וֹ וַיִּקַּ֖ח אֶת־הַֽמַּאֲכֶ֑לֶת לִשְׁחֹ֖ט אֶת־בְּנֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Avraham stretched forth his hand, and took the knife to slay his son.

notes.official:
The chapter's narrative-climax. The verse uses the verb *shachat* (*to slaughter, slay*) — the cultic-technical sacrificial-slaughter verb of Lev 1:5, 11; 3:2; 4:24; 14:13 etc. The vocabulary continues v 9's cultic-technical saturation: the act about to happen is named in the precise vocabulary of the Levitical sacrificial system.

The second of the chapter's two occurrences of *ma'akhelet* (the slaughter-knife — see [ma-akhelet-sacrificial-knife](#ma-akhelet-sacrificial-knife)). The cross-corpus pairing with Judg 19:29 (the Levite's dismembering of the concubine) is editorially load-bearing: both narratives use the rare *ma'akhelet* at moments of (potential or actual) human-victim slaughter (Sarna 1989; Trible *Texts of Terror* 1984 ch. 3).

*Va-yishlach Avraham et-yado* (*and Avraham stretched forth his hand*) is the action-verb that the messenger's intervention at v 12 will explicitly reverse — *al-tishlach yadkha el-ha-na'ar* (*do not lay your hand upon the lad*). The narrative is structured around the verb *shalach yad*: Avraham extends; the messenger forbids.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֨א אֵלָ֜יו מַלְאַ֤ךְ יְהוָה֙ מִן־הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אַבְרָהָ֣ם ׀ אַבְרָהָ֑ם וַיֹּ֖אמֶר הִנֵּֽנִי׃

i18n.en: And the messenger of YHWH called to him out of heaven, and said, Avraham, Avraham. And he said, Here am I.

notes.official:
The chapter's staying-of-the-hand. Two editorially-marked formulae converge at this verse: the **doubled-name vocative** *Avraham Avraham*, and the **third *hineni*** of the chapter's threefold structure.

***Avraham Avraham***. The doubled-name divine vocation-call recurs at exactly four moments in the Hebrew Bible — naming the four foundational vocational-calls of the canonical narrative: **Gen 22:11** (Avraham, this verse); **Gen 46:2** (*Ya'aqov Ya'aqov*, the night-vision before the descent to Egypt — the closest parallel-formulation, including the *hineni* response); **Exod 3:4** (*Moshe Moshe*, the burning bush — the parallel-formulation in precise lexical parallel: *va-yiqra elav* + doubled name + *hineni*); **1 Sam 3:10** (*Sh'mu'el Sh'mu'el*, the call of the prophet). The four-fold pattern names the canonical figures of patriarchal foundation, Israel-name foundation, exodus foundation, and monarchy-transition foundation. The Masoretic *paseq* (the vertical-stroke separator visible in the MT at this verse — *Avraham | Avraham*) editorially marks the doubling. **Genesis Rabbah 56:7** reads the doubled-vocative as *l'shon chibah u-l'shon zeruz* — *an expression of affection and an expression of urgency*. See [doubled-name-calling-formula](#doubled-name-calling-formula) for the full cross-corpus apparatus and the NT-reception (Acts 9:4 / 22:7 / 26:14 — *Saoul Saoul*, the Damascus-road call of Paul; Luke 10:41 *Martha Martha*; Luke 22:31 *Simon Simon*; Luke 13:34 / Matt 23:37 *Ierousalēm Ierousalēm*).

***Va-yomer hineni***. The third *hineni* — the response to the messenger's call. The threefold structure (Elohim at v 1; Yitzchaq at v 7; the messenger at v 11) is the chapter's structural-rhythmic backbone (see [hineni-prophetic-response-formula](#hineni-prophetic-response-formula)).

***Mal'akh YHWH***. The messenger of YHWH — first introduced in the Avraham cycle at Gen 16 — returns at this chapter's pivot. The modern critical literature presents three parallel positions on the messenger-identity question (Heidt 1949's distinct-envoy reading; Westermann 1985 / von Rad 1972's identity reading; Hamori 2008 / Sommer 2009 / MacDonald 2009's literary-theological-device reading); the WoH translation *messenger of YHWH* (preserving the Hebrew etymology over the conventional *angel*) is editorially neutral on the identity question. See [malakh-yhwh-messenger](#malakh-yhwh-messenger). The figure recurs at v 15 (the second call); the chapter's deeper structural seam is the v 11 / v 15 messenger-bracketing of the substitution-and-oath sequence.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אַל־תִּשְׁלַ֤ח יָֽדְךָ֙ אֶל־הַנַּ֔עַר וְאַל־תַּ֥עַשׂ ל֖וֹ מְא֑וּמָּה כִּ֣י ׀ עַתָּ֣ה יָדַ֗עְתִּי כִּֽי־יְרֵ֤א אֱלֹהִים֙ אַ֔תָּה וְלֹ֥א חָשַׂ֛כְתָּ אֶת־בִּנְךָ֥ אֶת־יְחִידְךָ֖ מִמֶּֽנִּי׃

i18n.en: And he said, Do not lay your hand upon the lad, neither do anything to him; for now I know that you fear the Elohim, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.

notes.official:
The chapter's verdict and the theological-engine of the test. Three philological-and-theological cruxes converge.

***Atah yadati*** — *now I know*. The phrase generates the classical theological-problem of divine testing: if the deity is omniscient, what does the test produce? Four scholarly positions parallel: (a) **Maimonides** *Guide* III.24 reads the test as pedagogical-demonstration *l-hodi'a* (to make known) to humanity, not for the deity's information; (b) the **patristic / disclosure reading** (Augustine, Aquinas *ST* I q.14, II-II q.97) distinguishes the deity's foreknowledge from the test's function of disclosing the latent disposition in publicly-visible form; (c) the **open-theism position** (Pinnock 1994; Sanders 1998; Boyd 2000) reads the *atah yadati* literally as a real epistemic event; (d) the **modern critical default** (Sarna 1989 p. 153; Westermann 1985 pp. 361-362; Wenham 1994 p. 110; Hamilton 1995 p. 113; Brueggemann 1982 pp. 187-194; von Rad 1972 pp. 244-245) reads the *atah yadati* as narrative-anthropomorphism — the chapter is a story in the strict literary sense, and the story requires the test-and-discover narrative-grammar. The four positions are documented; none is preempted at the translation level. See [ata-yadati-divine-learning-question](#ata-yadati-divine-learning-question) for the full apparatus, including the Heschel-pathos framework and the Kierkegaardian-existential and Levinasian-Derridean continental-philosophical receptions (flagged-downstream).

***Yere Elohim atah*** — *you fear the Elohim*. The chapter's certification of Avraham as a *yere Elohim* — *fearer of the Elohim* — is the structural inversion of Gen 20:11, where Avraham himself had pre-judged Gerar as lacking the fear-of-the-Elohim. The patriarch who at Gen 20:11 had wrongly assumed the foreign land lacked the moral-restraint motif is here at Gen 22:12 himself certified as one who fears the Elohim, the certification coming from the deity at the climax of the *aqedah*. The motif's cross-corpus distribution (Exod 1:17, 1:21 the Hebrew midwives; Exod 18:21 Yitro's judges; Exod 20:20 post-Sinai; Job 1:1, 1:8, 2:3 Job's characterization; Prov 1:7, 9:10 the wisdom-tradition motto; Eccl 12:13 Qohelet's summa) is documented at [yirat-elohim-moral-restraint-motif](#yirat-elohim-moral-restraint-motif). Becker 1965 is the foundational monographic treatment.

***V-lo chasakhta et-binkha et-yechidkha mimeni*** — the verb *chasakh* (*to withhold*) recurs at v 16 in the same clause, framing the chapter's verdict in repeated-key vocabulary. *Yechidkha* (*your only one*) is the chapter's recurring designation of Yitzchaq (vv 2, 12, 16); see [yechid-only-one-formula](#yechid-only-one-formula) for the narrative-internal Yishma'el-tension and the three modern critical readings (covenant-line, affective-emotional, combined).

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשָּׂ֨א אַבְרָהָ֜ם אֶת־עֵינָ֗יו וַיַּרְא֙ וְהִנֵּה־אַ֔יִל אַחַ֕ר נֶאֱחַ֥ז בַּסְּבַ֖ךְ בְּקַרְנָ֑יו וַיֵּ֤לֶךְ אַבְרָהָם֙ וַיִּקַּ֣ח אֶת־הָאַ֔יִל וַיַּעֲלֵ֥הוּ לְעֹלָ֖ה תַּ֥חַת בְּנֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Avraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold, behind him a ram caught in the thicket by his horns: and Avraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt-offering in the stead of his son.

notes.official:
The chapter's substitution-pivot. The (averted) human-sacrifice is replaced by an animal-substitution — an *ayil* (ram), the standard *olah*-class sacrificial animal (Lev 1:10; 5:15, 18; 6:6; 9:2-4; 16:3-5 — the Yom Kippur ritual with two rams; 23:18; Ezek 43-46). The same sacrificial-class is preserved across the substitution-pivot: the substitute is itself an *olah*-class animal, marking the substitution as a *class-preserving* exchange.

**The substitutionary-sacrifice theology**. The substitution is the foundation of the rabbinic *zecher aqedat Yitzchaq* (*memorial of the binding*) tradition and the wider *zechut avot* (*merit of the fathers*) tradition (Genesis Rabbah 56:9; b. Rosh Hashanah 16a). The *shofar* (ram's-horn) of the Rosh Hashanah liturgy is connected to the *qarnei ha-ayil* (the ram's horns) of this verse — the *shofar*-blast invokes the *aqedah*-merit (Spiegel 1967; Levenson 1993 chs 7-10; Vermes 1973). The **Christian vicarious-atonement reception** reads the ram-substitution as the typological foundation of the doctrine of vicarious atonement (Hebrews 11:17-19; Origen *Homilies on Genesis* VIII; Augustine; the Reformation atonement-theology — Luther, Calvin; Daly 1978; Lerch 1950). The **Islamic reception** (Sura 37:107 *dhibhin azim* — *a mighty sacrifice*; the early tafsir tradition treats the ram as a special-divine-provision). All three reception-traditions are flagged-not-preempted. See [ayil-ram-substitution-achar-echad-variant](#ayil-ram-substitution-achar-echad-variant).

**The textual variant *achar* / *echad***. The MT reads *achar* (אַחַר) — *behind / after* — supported by the Samaritan Pentateuch and Onkelos. The LXX (*kai idou krios heis*), Peshitta (*chad*), and some Vulgate manuscripts read *echad* (אֶחָד) — *one*. The variant rests on the visually-similar *resh / dalet* (ר/ד) confusion. Modern critical positions divide: **Sarna**, **Wenham**, **Hamilton** preserve MT *achar* as lectio difficilior; **Speiser** 1964 p. 163 and **Westermann** 1985 pp. 360-361 (cautiously) read LXX *echad* as original; **Skinner** and **Driver** treat the variant as unresolvable. The WoH translation preserves the MT *achar* (*behind him*) per established textual-conservative practice.

The second occurrence of the *sa eynav va-yar* (*lifted up his eyes and saw*) formula in the chapter (the first at v 4), framing Avraham's two seeings — the place from afar (v 4) and the substitute ram (v 13) — as the chapter's structural seeing-arc. See [sa-eynekha-lift-your-eyes](#sa-eynekha-lift-your-eyes).

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֧א אַבְרָהָ֛ם שֵֽׁם־הַמָּק֥וֹם הַה֖וּא יְהוָ֣ה ׀ יִרְאֶ֑ה אֲשֶׁר֙ יֵאָמֵ֣ר הַיּ֔וֹם בְּהַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה יֵרָאֶֽה׃

i18n.en: And Avraham called the name of that place YHWH-yir'eh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of YHWH it shall be provided.

notes.official:
The chapter's etiological-closing-formula. The place-name *YHWH-yir'eh* (*YHWH-will-see / YHWH-will-provide*) preserves the chapter's r-'-h wordplay-axis in proper-name form. The verbal element *yir'eh* (qal active 3ms imperfect of *r-'-h*) retains the seeing-and-providing identity from Avraham's v 8 statement (*Elohim yir'eh-lo ha-seh*); the verse's first half is the place-name proper.

The closing-formula *b-har YHWH yera'eh* — *on the mountain of YHWH it shall be seen / he shall appear / it shall be provided* — introduces a deliberate verbal shift. *Yera'eh* is the **niphal** 3ms imperfect of *r-'-h* — the same form used in the patriarchal-theophany formula *va-yera YHWH* (see [va-yera-yhwh-theophany](#va-yera-yhwh-theophany)). The shift from active *yir'eh* (v 14a) to passive *yera'eh* (v 14b) enacts the chapter's deepest theological move: the deity who *sees-and-provides* (active) is the same deity who *will-appear / will-be-seen* (passive) at the place. The seeing-and-being-seen identity is the engine of the chapter's wordplay-axis. See [yireh-yerah-hreh-wordplay](#yireh-yerah-hreh-wordplay) for the full active/passive analysis across the chapter's five-fold *r-'-h* distribution (vv 4, 8, 13, 14a, 14b).

The **Chronicler's identification** at 2 Chr 3:1 (*va-yachel Shlomoh livnot et-beit YHWH bi-Yrushalayim b-har ha-Moriah asher nir'ah l-David aviv*) explicitly reuses the same r-'-h root in the niphal (*nir'ah* — *appeared / was-seen*), marking the cross-reference between this verse's *b-har YHWH yera'eh* and the David-and-Temple-Mount appearance-tradition (2 Sam 24:16-25; 1 Chr 21:15-30). The temple-mount identification is foundational to the Jewish tradition (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan to Gen 22:14 explicitly identifies *har ha-Moriah* with the Temple-Mount). The Christian and Islamic reception-engagements are documented at [eretz-ha-moriah-temple-mount-identification](#eretz-ha-moriah-temple-mount-identification).

The etiological-formula *asher ye'amer ha-yom* (*as it is said to this day*) is a Hebrew Bible etiological marker (cf. 1 Sam 5:5; 2 Sam 18:18) indicating that the place-name was preserved as a continuing-tradition in the narrator's contemporary world. **Sarna** 1989 p. 154; **Westermann** 1985 pp. 363-364; **Hamilton** 1995 pp. 113-114.

The WoH translation preserves the transliterated place-name *YHWH-yir'eh* and reads *it shall be provided* at the closing-formula (ASV-baseline). The wordplay-axis is carried in the apparatus; the translation cannot preserve the *see-equals-provide* identity that Hebrew *r-'-h* carries.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֛א מַלְאַ֥ךְ יְהוָ֖ה אֶל־אַבְרָהָ֑ם שֵׁנִ֖ית מִן־הַשָּׁמָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: And the messenger of YHWH called to Avraham a second time out of heaven,

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר בִּ֥י נִשְׁבַּ֖עְתִּי נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה כִּ֗י יַ֚עַן אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָשִׂ֙יתָ֙ אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה וְלֹ֥א חָשַׂ֖כְתָּ אֶת־בִּנְךָ֥ אֶת־יְחִידֶֽךָ׃

i18n.en: and said, By myself I have sworn, says YHWH, because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son,

notes.official:
The chapter's climactic divine-oath. Two editorially-marked formulae converge in a single clause: the divine-self-oath *bi nishbati* (*by myself I have sworn*), and the prophetic-utterance formula *n'um YHWH* (*says YHWH* / *utterance of YHWH*).

***Bi nishbati*** — the divine-self-oath. The deity, having no superior by which to swear, swears by himself. The formula is rare and structurally-load-bearing across the canon. **Gen 22:16 is the first occurrence of the formula in canonical narrative**; the formula then recurs in the prophetic corpus: **Isa 45:23** (*every knee shall bow* — cited at Rom 14:11 and Phil 2:10-11 as the foundational NT-text of the universal-confession); **Jer 22:5, 49:13, 51:14**; **Amos 6:8** (with parallel *b-nafsho* — *by his life*); **Isa 62:8**. **Hebrews 6:13-14** explicitly cites Gen 22:16-17 as the locus of the divine self-oath: *epei kat' oudenos eichen meizonos omosai, ōmosen kath' heautou* — *since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself*. The Hebrews-reception is the foundational NT-treatment of the divine-self-oath as the theological-engine of the divine-promise-bond (Lane 1991; Attridge 1989; Ellingworth 1993). The reception is flagged-not-preempted; see [bi-nishbati-divine-self-oath](#bi-nishbati-divine-self-oath).

***N'um YHWH*** — the prophetic-utterance formula. *N'um YHWH* (*utterance of YHWH* / *declares YHWH*) is the standard prophetic-utterance formula, recurring approximately 365 times across the Hebrew Bible, overwhelmingly in the prophetic corpus (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the Twelve). **Gen 22:16 is the chronological-canonical first occurrence in the Hebrew Bible** — the formula's narrative-debut. The next occurrences (Num 14:28; 1 Sam 2:30; 2 Sam 23:1 — David's last words; 2 Kgs 9:26, 19:33) are concentrated in the early prophetic-narrative, before the formula's proliferation in the major and minor prophets. The lexeme *n'um* is morphologically a passive-participle of *n-'-m* (to utter), nominalized into a construct-noun; the lexeme is otherwise almost exclusively attested in the *n'um YHWH* / *n'um Adonai YHWH* formulae (HALOT ii.658-659; BDB p. 610). The first-canonical-occurrence at Gen 22:16 is therefore the foundational instance for the entire prophetic-utterance formula's HB distribution.

The *bi nishbati n'um YHWH* combination marks the chapter's blessing (vv 17-18) as a maximally-binding divine-pronouncement: the divine-self-oath (the strongest form of divine-commitment) combined with the prophetic-utterance-formula (the strongest form of divine-speech-act). The chapter's promise to Avraham is therefore the chapter's most-binding divine-statement — and its first-canonical-occurrence status marks the *aqedah* as the locus of the foundational divine-self-oath of the Hebrew Bible. **Cross** *Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic* 1973 ch. 11 on the divine-self-oath as covenantal-binding form; **Hillers** 1964 and **Weinfeld** 1972 on the wider ANE-and-Deuteronomic oath-and-treaty material.

The verbal echo of v 12 — *v-lo chasakhta et-binkha et-yechidkha* — recurs here at v 16 in slightly-varied form (*v-lo chasakhta et-binkha et-yechidekha*), framing the verdict-and-oath as a single semantic-unit with the certification of v 12. See [yechid-only-one-formula](#yechid-only-one-formula).

paragraphs.text: כִּֽי־בָרֵ֣ךְ אֲבָרֶכְךָ֗ וְהַרְבָּ֨ה אַרְבֶּ֤ה אֶֽת־זַרְעֲךָ֙ כְּכוֹכְבֵ֣י הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וְכַח֕וֹל אֲשֶׁ֖ר עַל־שְׂפַ֣ת הַיָּ֑ם וְיִרַ֣שׁ זַרְעֲךָ֔ אֵ֖ת שַׁ֥עַר אֹיְבָֽיו׃

i18n.en: that in blessing I will bless you, and in multiplying I will multiply your seed as the stars of the heavens, and as the sand which is upon the seashore; and your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies;

paragraphs.text: וְהִתְבָּרֲכ֣וּ בְזַרְעֲךָ֔ כֹּ֖ל גּוֹיֵ֣י הָאָ֑רֶץ עֵ֕קֶב אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁמַ֖עְתָּ בְּקֹלִֽי׃

i18n.en: and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth bless themselves; because you have obeyed my voice.

notes.official:
*V-hitbarakhu b-zarakha kol goyei ha-aretz* — the universal-blessing formula in **hithpael** pointing (*shall bless themselves*). The MT-fidelity policy ratified at Gen 12 (glossary entry [nivrakhu-bekha-niphal-hithpael](#nivrakhu-bekha-niphal-hithpael)) preserves the verse-by-verse niphal/hithpael distinction across the five universal-blessing-promise occurrences: niphal-pointed (passive *shall be blessed*) at Gen 12:3, 18:18, 28:14; hithpael-pointed (middle/reflexive *shall bless themselves*) at Gen 22:18 and 26:4.

Three positions parallel: (a) **Traditional Christian / Pauline reading** — the LXX renders all five verses with the passive *eneulogēthēsontai*; Paul cites the verse as straightforwardly passive in **Galatians 3:8**, reading the passive as the textual foundation of the gospel-to-the-gentiles; ASV/RSV/NRSV follow Paul. (b) **Modern critical consensus** (Speiser, Sarna, Westermann, NJPS) — the original idiom was middle/reflexive across all five verses (*by you all the families shall bless themselves* — i.e., invoke Avraham's name as a paradigm of blessing, cf. Gen 48:20). The niphal-pointings at 12:3 / 18:18 / 28:14 are Masoretic harmonization toward the theologically-richer passive. (c) **MT-preserving reading** (Wenham, Hamilton) — the distinction is meaningful and should be preserved verse-by-verse. The WoH translation follows position (c) — verse-by-verse, matching MT pointing at each occurrence.

The Pauline reception of Gal 3:8 (*proeuangelisato tō Abraam hoti eneulogēthēsontai en soi panta ta ethnē* — *the scripture preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, In you shall all the nations be blessed*) is flagged as downstream Greek-reception and is not preempted by the translation choice. See [nivrakhu-bekha-niphal-hithpael](#nivrakhu-bekha-niphal-hithpael) for the full apparatus.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֤שָׁב אַבְרָהָם֙ אֶל־נְעָרָ֔יו וַיָּקֻ֛מוּ וַיֵּלְכ֥וּ יַחְדָּ֖ו אֶל־בְּאֵ֣ר שָׁ֑בַע וַיֵּ֥שֶׁב אַבְרָהָ֖ם בִּבְאֵ֥ר שָֽׁבַע׃ (פ)

i18n.en: So Avraham returned to his young men, and they rose up and went together to Be'er Sheva; and Avraham dwelt at Be'er Sheva.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֗י אַחֲרֵי֙ הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה וַיֻּגַּ֥ד לְאַבְרָהָ֖ם לֵאמֹ֑ר הִ֠נֵּה יָלְדָ֨ה מִלְכָּ֥ה גַם־הִ֛וא בָּנִ֖ים לְנָח֥וֹר אָחִֽיךָ׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Avraham, saying, Behold, Milkah, she also has borne children to Nachor your brother:

paragraphs.text: אֶת־ע֥וּץ בְּכֹר֖וֹ וְאֶת־בּ֣וּז אָחִ֑יו וְאֶת־קְמוּאֵ֖ל אֲבִ֥י אֲרָֽם׃

i18n.en: Uts his firstborn, and Buz his brother, and Kemu'el the father of Aram,

paragraphs.text: וְאֶת־כֶּ֣שֶׂד וְאֶת־חֲז֔וֹ וְאֶת־פִּלְדָּ֖שׁ וְאֶת־יִדְלָ֑ף וְאֵ֖ת בְּתוּאֵֽל׃

i18n.en: and Kesed, and Chazo, and Pildash, and Yidlaf, and Betu'el.

paragraphs.text: וּבְתוּאֵ֖ל יָלַ֣ד אֶת־רִבְקָ֑ה שְׁמֹנָ֥ה אֵ֙לֶּה֙ יָלְדָ֣ה מִלְכָּ֔ה לְנָח֖וֹר אֲחִ֥י אַבְרָהָֽם׃

i18n.en: And Betu'el begat Rivkah: these eight Milkah bore to Nachor, Avraham's brother.

paragraphs.text: וּפִֽילַגְשׁ֖וֹ וּשְׁמָ֣הּ רְאוּמָ֑ה וַתֵּ֤לֶד גַּם־הִוא֙ אֶת־טֶ֣בַח וְאֶת־גַּ֔חַם וְאֶת־תַּ֖חַשׁ וְאֶֽת־מַעֲכָֽה׃ (ס)

i18n.en: And his concubine, whose name was Re'umah, she also bore Tevach, and Gacham, and Tachash, and Ma'akhah.
